observation.visible_scene: A fixed close-up of a small forest stream cascading over a rounded central boulder. Moss-covered rocks flank the right side, a decaying log sits at the upper left, and low green plants with scattered dry leaves and pine needles line the right bank. A thin sheet of water flows from the top over the central rock and breaks into white frothy turbulence at the lower left and center; a calmer dark pool with floating leaves lies on the right.
visible_changes: The water cascading over the central rock continuously changes its surface texture: the shimmering film, the thin vertical rivulets on the rock face, and the pattern of bubbles and white foam shift from frame to frame throughout the excerpt.
The churning pool of white water at the bottom left and bottom center keeps bubbling and reforming, with the boundary of the foam expanding and contracting slightly.
Small ripple rings appear and fade on the dark water surface of the right-side pool (notably mid-to-late frames), indicating ongoing surface disturbance.
A small orange-yellow leaf resting on a rock between the cascade and the mossy boulder stays in the same position across all frames (static, not moving with the water).
The single green leaf on the bottom-center rock, the moss patches, the plants on the right, and the log remain fixed in place.
The framing of all background elements is unchanged, indicating no camera movement during the segment.
outside_clip_unknowns: The upstream source feeding the thin top stream and the downstream continuation of the flow are not shown.
Whether wind or rain is acting on the plants and pools is not determinable from these frames.
The overall duration and any beginning or end of the cascade lie outside this cropped segment.
uncertain_details: The flow is already in progress at the first frame and continues at the last; no onset or completion of the cascade is captured.
Any motion of the green plants is too subtle to confirm as object movement versus compression or lighting change.
The exact rate and volume of the flow cannot be quantified from stills.
